summary.heading: What is a wave?
summary.html:
• A travelling wave transfers energy without any overall transfer of matter. Each particle of the medium oscillates about its own equilibrium position and ends up where it started.
  • A single disturbance is a pulse; a repeated one (often a source in SHM) gives a continuous wave.
  • Each particle oscillates at the source's frequency, slightly later than the particle before it.
  • The wave speed depends on the medium, not the source (faster on a tighter rope; faster for sound in water than in air).

summary.heading: Transverse and longitudinal waves
summary.html:
TransverseLongitudinal
Particles oscillateperpendicular to the direction of travelparallel to the direction of travel
Featurescrests and troughscompressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure)
Exampleswaves on a string, all EM wavessound, a push-pull pulse on a slinky

summary.heading: Wavelength, frequency and wave speed
summary.html:
• Wavelength $\lambda$: the shortest distance between two points moving in phase (crest to crest, compression to compression).
  • Period $T$: time for one oscillation of a particle; $f = 1/T$. Amplitude: maximum displacement.
  • In one period the wave moves forward one wavelength:
$$v = f\lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T}$$
  • The frequency is set by the source and doesn't change in a new medium. The speed is set by the medium, so if the speed changes, the wavelength changes in proportion.

summary.heading: Two kinds of wave graph
summary.html:
• Read the horizontal axis first. A displacement–distance graph (a snapshot) gives the wavelength; a displacement–time graph (one particle) gives the period.
  • Which way is a particle moving? Shift the snapshot slightly in the direction of travel and see whether the particle's displacement goes up or down.
  • Particles at crests and troughs are momentarily at rest; particles at equilibrium move fastest.
  • For a longitudinal wave, displacement means displacement along the direction of travel. A compression is where particles on both sides are displaced towards it.

summary.heading: Sound and electromagnetic waves
summary.html:
• Sound: a longitudinal mechanical wave that needs a medium (a bell in an evacuated jar goes silent). About 340 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ in air, faster in liquids (about 1500 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ in water) and solids. Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 kHz; above that is ultrasound. Pitch depends on frequency, loudness on amplitude.
  • EM waves: oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, so always transverse. Produced by accelerating charges; no medium needed; all travel at $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ in a vacuum.
RegionApproximate wavelength
Gammabelow about $10^{-11}$ m
X-rays$10^{-11}$ to $10^{-8}$ m
Ultraviolet$10^{-8}$ to $4 \times 10^{-7}$ m
Visible400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red)
Infrared$7 \times 10^{-7}$ to $10^{-3}$ m
Microwaves$10^{-3}$ to about $10^{-1}$ m
Radioabove about $10^{-1}$ m
  • From radio to gamma: wavelength decreases, frequency and photon energy increase. The boundaries aren't sharp.

summary.heading: Mechanical and EM waves compared; intensity
summary.html:
MechanicalElectromagnetic
What oscillatesparticles of the mediumelectric and magnetic fields
Medium needed?yesno
Typetransverse or longitudinalalways transverse
Speeddepends on the medium$c$ in a vacuum, slower in materials
  • Both transfer energy without net transfer of matter, obey $v = f\lambda$, and reflect, refract, diffract and interfere.
  • Intensity (power per unit area, $\text{W m}^{-2}$) from a point source: $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}$.
New for 2028 $$I \propto A^2$$
  • Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude: doubling $A$ gives four times the intensity. Combined with the inverse-square law, the amplitude from a point source falls as $A \propto \frac{1}{r}$.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Thinking the medium travels with the wave.
  • Reading a period off a displacement–distance graph, or a wavelength off a displacement–time graph.
  • Thinking the frequency changes when a wave enters a new medium.
  • Saying a higher frequency travels faster (in one medium it just has a shorter wavelength).
  • Calling sound transverse, or saying EM waves need a medium.
  • Measuring a wavelength from a crest to the next trough (that is half a wavelength).

Models: List the quantities in the wave model. Which of them mean something different for sound, for a rope and for light?
Why is it powerful when one model fits very different situations? Can students think of a case where the wave model fails?
Theories: Maxwell predicted a speed from electrical and magnetic measurements, and it matched the speed of light. Why is a prediction that matches an independent measurement such strong evidence?
Hertz confirmed the prediction about 20 years later. Was the theory scientific knowledge before that?
Observations: Röntgen noticed something he wasn't looking for. What prepares a scientist to recognise an accidental discovery as important?
X-rays were in hospitals within months, before anyone understood the risks. What does that tell us about how new discoveries should be used?

oracy.html:
Odd one out (pairs, 6 minutes, then share): each pair justifies one choice, then argues for a different one. Items: sound in air, a wave on a guitar string, microwaves, visible light.

  • The odd one out is … because …
  • But you could also argue …
  • The other three all …

Listen for: each choice names a property: sound is the only longitudinal wave; only microwaves and light can travel through a vacuum, at $c$; the string wave and sound are mechanical and need a medium.

Can something wave if nothing is waving?: The ether was widely believed for decades. Why did physicists find a wave with no medium so hard to accept?
If part of a model turns out not to exist, should we keep the parts that still work?
How do instruments extend what we can kn: Show a thermal camera image or a radio telescope image. Is this "seeing", or a picture built from data?
What do we have to trust (about the instrument and its makers) to accept what it shows?
Similar maths, same thing?: Sound and light share $v = f\lambda$, but one needs a medium and one doesn't. Is the shared equation a deep similarity or a coincidence of form?
Ask students for other places where the same equation describes different things (for example inverse-square laws in gravity, electricity and light).
Who should benefit from a discovery?: Röntgen refused a patent. Compare this with modern medical technologies that are patented. Which approach helps more people in the long run?
Should publicly funded research be free for everyone to use?
